title: An RGB LED cycles red, green, blue

turns.user: Make the RGB LED cycle through red, green and blue, on GPIO17, GPIO27 and GPIO22.
turns.assistant:
Now the code:I've built the circuit and written the code. ERC shows 0 errors and 0 warnings, and the code check says it matches the wiring.

**What you built**
- **LED:** the kit's common-cathode RGB LED (D1) sits in column b, rows 40–43: red in 40, cathode in 41, green in 42, blue in 43.
- **Resistors:** each colour has its own resistor across the centre gap, from column e to column f.
  - R1 is 220 Ω, red, in row 40.
  - R2 is 100 Ω, green, in row 42.
  - R3 is 100 Ω, blue, in row 43.
- **Leads:**
  - GPIO17 goes to 40j, GPIO27 to 42j, GPIO22 to 43j.
  - GND runs from 41a to row 20.

**How it works**
The three colours share one negative leg (the cathode), which goes to ground. Each colour turns on when its GPIO goes HIGH. The program lights red, then green, then blue, one second each, and keeps cycling. Ctrl+C stops it and turns all three off. In the code test, GPIO17, GPIO27 and GPIO22 each went high for 1.000 s in turn.

**Why the resistor values differ**
- **Red:** (3.3 − 2.0 V) / 220 Ω ≈ 5.9 mA. The simulation gave **5.3 mA** on GPIO17.
- **Green and blue:** these need about 3.0 V to light, so a 3.3 V pin has only about 0.3 V left for the resistor. With 220 Ω they got only 1.3 mA and would look dim. At 100 Ω the simulation gives **2.2 mA** each. A smaller resistor gains very little, because the problem is the 3.3 V supply, not the resistor. So expect green and blue to look a bit dimmer than red.
- Only one colour is on at a time, so the most any pin carries is 5.3 mA. That's well under the 16 mA per-pin limit.

**What to check on the bench**
- **LED direction:** the **longest leg is the common cathode** and goes in row 41, the one with the GND lead. The single leg on its own side of it is red (row 40). Green and blue are the two on the other side (rows 42, 43).
- **Resistors:** make sure each one really crosses the centre gap (e to f). If both ends sit in the same half-row, it does nothing.
- **100 Ω resistors:** if your kit has no 100 Ω, 220 Ω works too. Green and blue will just be dimmer.
- **Ribbon:** the stripe on the ribbon cable goes to pin 1, at the 3V3 end of the T-board, on both the Pi and the T-board.

I couldn't take a picture of the layout to check it by eye: this session has no 3D view. I checked the positions from the hole list instead.

input.source:
import time
import RPi.GPIO as GPIO

# BCM numbers. Common-cathode LED, so HIGH = colour on.
RED = 17
GREEN = 27
BLUE = 22
STEP_S = 1.0  # seconds per colour

GPIO.setmode(GPIO.BCM)
GPIO.setup(RED, GPIO.OUT, initial=GPIO.LOW)
GPIO.setup(GREEN, GPIO.OUT, initial=GPIO.LOW)
GPIO.setup(BLUE, GPIO.OUT, initial=GPIO.LOW)

COLOURS = [("red", RED), ("green", GREEN), ("blue", BLUE)]

try:
    while True:
        for name, pin in COLOURS:
            print(name)
            GPIO.output(pin, GPIO.HIGH)
            time.sleep(STEP_S)
            GPIO.output(pin, GPIO.LOW)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass
finally:
    GPIO.cleanup()
